questions.prompt: Match each property to its meaning.

pairs.right: Can be hammered into thin sheets
Makes a ringing sound when struck

questions.explain: Metals are malleable, ductile, sonorous and lustrous; many non-metals are brittle.

questions.prompt: Sort these elements into metals and non-metals.
questions.explain: Mercury is a (liquid) metal; iodine is a (shiny) non-metal.
Graphite conducts electricity: an important exception, used in batteries and pencils.

questions.prompt: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
questions.explain: Mercury melts at −39 °C, so it's liquid at room temperature.

questions.prompt: Match each use to the property it depends on.
Why are cooking pots made of metal but their handles made of plastic or wood?
options: Metal conducts heat to cook food; plastic and wood are poor conductors, so the handle stays cool
questions.explain: Conductors heat the food; insulators protect your hand.

questions.prompt: A material is shiny, brittle and does not conduct electricity. It is most likely…
questions.explain: Brittle and non-conducting point to a non-metal; shininess alone isn't enough to call it a metal.

questions.text: The ability of metals to be drawn into thin wires is called ___, and to be beaten into sheets is called ___.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to test whether a material conducts electricity.
steps: Build a circuit with a battery, bulb and wires, leaving a gap
Check the bulb lights when the wires touch
Place the material across the gap
questions.explain: Always check your circuit works first, so a dark bulb really means 'does not conduct'.

questions.prompt: Diamond and graphite are both made of carbon. Explain why graphite is called an 'exception' among non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Non-metals are usually poor conductors of electricity, but graphite conducts electricity well. So graphite breaks the general rule for non-metals, even though it is made of carbon like diamond (which does not conduct).
rubric: So it breaks the general rule
questions.explain: Exceptions show why scientists look at many properties, not one.
